Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
I only bought a couple of Bloodlines boosters yesterday as a sample.
But I looked over the 8 boosters that another player here bought.
Some comments

1. the Daughters of Cacophony look quite cool - better than the usual
Shy art and the frame helps.

2. we got a good laugh out of the Blood Brother, Tom. Our Tom here
(Tom Kassel) actually comes from Chicago.

3. The player who'd bought most boosters was mystified by all the new
disciplines. I was able to give him some clues because I seen the web
previews. Now that I check, I see that the wrappers say that there's
a rules sheet in every box. That's a sneaky way of making you buy a
whole box. I might do that now though as some cards do look quite
spiffy - notably the Mark V and Walking through Mountains (or whatever
it's called).

4. It's funny that the standard Cold Iron weapon - the Poker - is
actually illustrated as being red hot. And using it to slice
someone's head off seems rather implausible - it's a blunt instrument,
not a sword.

5. The layout guy is still having trouble getting things the right
size. The superior disciple symbols are too small because they've
been made the same height as the inferior. They should be about 40%
taller to make the squares the same size (c.f. Pythagorus). There's
generally so much fine print that this game is only playable by
daylight, AFAIC - not what you'd expect from a game about vampires.

Andrew

On Fri, 07 Dec 2001 08:16:37 -0500, LSJ wrote:

>> 4. It's funny that the standard Cold Iron weapon - the Poker - is
>> actually illustrated as being red hot.
>
>You're mistaking blood-stained for red hot. Red hot would not be so dark
>(like a blood stain).

I'm not sure what colour Kindred vitae is but human blood is darker
than illustrated while hot iron's shade varies with its temperature.
You're probably right about the intent though - it just wasn't what I
thought when I looked at the card.

I'm not convinced you've got the metallurgy right though. A poker
would be tend to be wrought-iron rather than cast-iron (beaten into
shape rather than poured into a mould). This would make it malleable
rather than brittle and so it is not going to break when it hits Skin
of Steel - it's just going to bend. This is sensible for a slender
tool which is designed to poke fires - you don't want it to fracture
when you do so. Here's a literary scene which comes to mind...

"Holmes chuckled heartily. "Your conversation is most entertaining,"
said he. "When you go out close the door, for there is a decided
draught."

"I will go when I have said my say. Don't you dare to meddle with my
affairs. I know that Miss Stoner has been here. I traced her! I am a
dangerous man to fall foul of! See here." He stepped swiftly forward,
seized the poker, and bent it into a curve with his huge brown hands.

"See that you keep yourself out of my grip," he snarled, and hurling
the twisted poker into the fireplace he strode out of the room.

"He seems a very amiable person," said Holmes, laughing. "I am not
quite so bulky, but if he had remained I might have shown him that my
grip was not much more feeble than his own." As he spoke he picked up
the steel poker and, with a sudden effort, straightened it out again."

Gripping stuff!

Andrew

Messages.Author: John
Messages.Body:
Just to weigh in with my 2 cents.

And if I'm wrong shoot me, I slept through several materials classes.

The process does not determine the hardness alone, too many other
factors are involved.

In general the process of "banging it into shape" is known as cold or
hot working, depending on whether it is done while the metal is heated
or to what degree. These processes can cause a phenomena called strain
hardening where the material becomes harder, but more brittle. I seem
to recall that it is the effect of the grains becoming elongated and
aligned in a linear fasion.

I believe cold iron would fall under cold working (and thus the name)

Pouring molten iron into a mold can produce a very soft material. The
heat makes the grains of the metal uniform and round creating a
material that is strong in terms of tensile strength but soft and
malleable.

So to review... I guess they cold forged that poker, probably more
than it should have been.

I've rambled on for a bit now, but if anyone cares I could dig up a
textbook or two and double check.

-JTP

From the searches available at http://dictionary.oed.com/ once that huge
subscription fee is paid.

(From cold.)

b. of material substances which in their natural state communicate
this sensation by contact. Often as a descriptive epithet of iron or
steel, as the material of a weapon. Hence, such combinations as ice-
cold, key-cold, stone-cold. See these words.

c1290 Lives Saints (1887) 183 So cold ase a ston. 1297 R. GLOUC.
(1724) 1 Welles swete and colde. 1576 FLEMING Panoplie Ep. 231 Blowe
hot and colde breath out of one mouth. 1667 MILTON P.L. x. 851
Outstretcht he lay, on the cold ground. 1771 SMOLLETT Humph. Cl. (1796)
II. 36 To hazard a thrust of cold iron with his antagonist. 1795
MACNEILL Will & Jean II. x, Wi' the cauld ground for his bed. 1816 SCOTT
Old Mort. xvi, Try him with the cold steel. 1833 MARRYAT P. Simple
xxxiii, Others darted cold shot at us.

(From iron.)

1665 SIR T. HERBERT Trav. (1677) 131 Undertakes to
make the Turk eat cold Iron.

That's about all I can find with a cursory search. It doesn't tend to
deal, of course, with the concept of cold iron as put forward regarding
fae, which isn't an entirely new one but does tend to avoid obvious
sources of reference for the OED etc, to the best of my knowledge.

If anyone's reading The Mabinogion, the use of iron in the tale in
Branwen Uerch Ly+r is fairly interesting, especially given the Irish
connections.

Castle Falkenstein appears to have some references to this being iron
from space, from what I can tell.

(It's also useful to note that, in context, cold iron for V:TES in this
context (the Kiasyd) will draw on what cold iron is in the WoD, so other
discussions are somewhat academic.)

>I still reckon that you would either make a poker out of steel or
>wrought iron. The VTES poker therefore gets it wrong by suggesting
>that it will shatter when it hits skin of steel/marble/rock.

Burning it doesn't necessarily require that it shatter. For instance,
it could just be that it's bent so far that it's considered unusable.

It also seems possible that the idea is thematically inspired in order
to balance it, relative to items like Brass Knuckles, Garotte and
Bastard Sword, where some of the "realism" has been sacrificed so that a
card of a roughly equivalent power level is created.
